node.label: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
node.date_label: Of Grammatology (translation) 1976 · “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography” 1985 · “Three Women’s Texts” 1985 · “Can the Subaltern Speak?” 1988 · A Critique of Postcolonial Reason 1999
node.description: A literary theorist and the translator of Derrida’s Of Grammatology (1976), whose essays on colonial India became reference points for historians. In ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ (1985) she read the collective ‘from within but against the grain’, proposing that its recovery of subaltern consciousness be read ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’, and argued that it overlooked ‘how important the concept-metaphor woman is’ to its own discourse. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988) separates representation as ‘speaking for’ from ‘re-presentation’, argues that in Foucault and Deleuze’s conversation intellectuals, ‘representing them, ... represent themselves as transparent’, and reads the British abolition of sati through the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, set against the nativist ‘The women actually wanted to die’: between them ‘One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness.’ She later called the essay’s closing ‘the subaltern cannot speak!’ ‘an inadvisable remark’ (1999). In period, Gyan Prakash (1992) held that she ‘very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman’ as a limit of historical understanding, Rosalind O’Hanlon (1988) urged hesitation ‘before accepting’ her proposal to re-inscribe the series’ strategy ‘as a strategy for our times’, and Terry Eagleton (1999), crediting the book with addressing ‘the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’, found her Critique ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ and ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (b. 1942); translator’s preface to Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1976); “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography” (Subaltern Studies IV, 1985; introduction to Selected Subaltern Studies, 1988); “Three Women’s Texts and a Critique of Imperialism” (Critical Inquiry, 1985); “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (in Nelson and Grossberg, eds., Marxism and the Interpretation of Culture, 1988; revised in A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, 1999); “The New Subaltern: A Silent Interview” (2000). Readings: O’Hanlon (1988); Chakrabarty (1992); Prakash (1992); Sarkar (1994); Pandey (1995); Eagleton (1999); Chatterjee (2010).
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ in the 1988 text as reprinted in Williams and Chrisman, Colonial Discourse and Post-Colonial Theory (1993; pp. 66–111, opening abridged), with page numbers of that reprint; two 1988 page anchors (p. 277 and p. 308) come from Chakrabarty (1992, n. 48) and Sunder Rajan (2010). The 1999 revision was read in Morris’s 2010 reprint, which has no page numbers. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ was read in Subaltern Studies IV (1985), pp. 330–363, in full; ‘Three Women’s Texts’ pp. 243–245; the translator’s preface to Of Grammatology at p. lxxvii of the 1997 corrected edition. She is a literary critic, not a historian, and is not presented as a founder of postcolonial studies; she joined the Subaltern Studies editorial collective in the 1990s (Chaturvedi gives Subaltern Studies IX, 1996; Chatterjee recalls 1993) and in 2000 called herself ‘a sometime member’. Benita Parry’s in-period critique (Oxford Literary Review, 1987), Aijaz Ahmad’s In Theory (1992) and Lata Mani’s work on sati (1987, 1998) were not read; Ahmad appears only through Eagleton’s report of her contrast with him. Chatterjee (2010) is a later reading by a member of the collective and carries no in-period claim.

proposed_edges.relationship: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’: the two senses of representation, the epistemic violence of colonial law and knowledge, and the subaltern woman silenced between colonial and indigenous patriarchal discourse on sati (1985–99)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988), read in the Williams and Chrisman reprint (pages of that reprint; its opening is abridged): ‘Some of the most radical criticism coming out of the West today is the result of an interested desire to conserve the subject of the West, or the West as Subject’ (p. 66). ‘Two senses of representation are being run together: representation as “speaking for”, as in politics, and representation as “re-presentation”, as in art or philosophy’; ‘representing them, the intellectuals represent themselves as transparent’ (p. 70); running vertreten and darstellen together ‘leads to an essentialist, utopian politics’ (p. 71). The codification of Hindu law is her ‘example of epistemic violence’ (pp. 76–77), and she asks whether, ‘inside and outside the circuit of the epistemic violence of imperialist law and education’, ‘can the subaltern speak?’ (p. 78). On sati she sets the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, which she says she ‘put together’ (p. 92), against ‘the Indian nativist argument’, ‘“The women actually wanted to die”’: ‘The two sentences go a long way to legitimize each other. One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness’ (p. 93). She qualifies: ‘Given that the abolition of sati was in itself admirable’ (p. 94); ‘Obviously I am not advocating the killing of widows’ (p. 97). ‘Between patriarchy and imperialism, subject-constitution and object-formation, the figure of the woman disappears ... into a violent shuttling’ (p. 102). She welcomes ‘all the information retrieval in these silenced areas’ in history and other disciplines, while warning that the assumed ‘consciousness or subject’ will ‘cohere with the work of imperialist subject-constitution’ (p. 90). The close: ‘The subaltern cannot speak. There is no virtue in global laundry lists with “woman” as a pious item. Representation has not withered away’ (reprint p. 104, OCR damaged, wording restored from the unpaginated 1988 text in Morris, 2010; 1988 p. 308 per Sunder Rajan in the same volume). She credits Lata Mani’s 1983 thesis on sati as ‘a brilliant account’ and ‘profited from discussion with Ms Mani’ (n. 65, p. 109). The 1999 revision (A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, ch. 3; read in Morris’s unpaginated reprint; CPR p. 308 per Sunder Rajan) says: ‘in the first version of this text, I wrote, in the accents of passionate lament: the subaltern cannot speak! It was an inadvisable remark’, and that Bhubaneswari Bhaduri ‘was not a “true” subaltern’. ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (Critical Inquiry, 1985, read pp. 243–245) opens: ‘It should not be possible to read nineteenth-century British literature without remembering that imperialism, understood as England’s social mission, was a crucial part of the cultural representation of England to the English’, and finds it ‘particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism’ (p. 243). In-period readings by historians: Gyan Prakash, ‘Can the “Subaltern” Ride?’ (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint 2000, pp. 226–227, read): ‘as Spivak states starkly, the debate left no room for the woman’s enunciatory position’; ‘Spivak very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman as the point at which the interpreter must acknowledge the limits of historical understanding’. Sumit Sarkar, ‘Orientalism Revisited’ (Oxford Literary Review, 1994; reprint p. 254, n. 14, read), criticising Mani’s Saidian assumptions, contrasts ‘the much more substantive discussion of pre-colonial and colonial discourses on sati in Spivak’. Contested in period: Terry Eagleton (LRB, 13 May 1999; web text, no page numbers, read) on A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ to be the critique its title promises, ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’, yet ‘this study boldly addresses the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’; he reports that she contrasts her own critique with Aijaz Ahmad’s ‘scorching assault’ in In Theory (1992; unread here). Benita Parry, ‘Problems in Current Theories of Colonial Discourse’, Oxford Literary Review 9 (1987), pp. 27–58, is the best-known in-period critique; it is closed access and unread, and no claim is made about its argument. A contribution, not a founding: the post entry already lists Said (1978) before her, and edge_107 (language → post) and edge_115 (subaltern → post) stay.

proposed_edges.relationship: A critique from within: the collective's recovery of subaltern consciousness read as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', Guha's 'full autonomy' questioned, and woman shown to be 'the neglected syntagm' of its accounts of insurgency (1985–88)
proposed_edges.map_label: Strategic essentialism and the gendered subaltern, 1985–88
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’, Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363, read in full: the group ‘offers a theory of change’, plotting change ‘as confrontations rather than transition’ (p. 330); its practice is ‘closer to deconstruction’ than its self-description (p. 332); ‘This is why I hope to align them with deconstruction’ (p. 336). ‘Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain’ (p. 341), she reads the project to retrieve subaltern consciousness ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’ (p. 342), which ‘would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness’ (p. 356). On gender: ‘The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women’, but ‘I think they overlook how important the concept-metaphor woman is to the functioning of their discourse’ (p. 356); ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357); ‘Male subaltern and historian are here united in the common assumption that the procreative sex is a species apart’ (p. 358); ‘woman is the neglected syntagm of the semiosis of subalternity of insurgency’ (p. 359); ‘if the question of female subaltern consciousness ... is a red herring, the question of subaltern consciousness as such must be judged a red herring as well’ (p. 360). She qualifies: ‘The making-visible of the figure of woman is perhaps not a task that the group should fairly be asked to perform’, but ‘a feminist historian of the subaltern must raise the question of woman as a structural rather than marginal issue’ (p. 361). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha’s ‘autonomous domain’, ‘I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy’ (p. 79); ‘the colonized subaltern subject is irretrievably heterogeneous’ (p. 79); ‘If, in the context of colonial production, the subaltern has no history and cannot speak, the subaltern as female is even more deeply in shadow’ (pp. 82–83). In-period readings from historians of the field: Rosalind O’Hanlon, ‘Recovering the Subject’ (Modern Asian Studies, 1988; Verso reprint, read), takes up her phrase (p. 80, citing SS IV p. 342) but warns ‘we should certainly hesitate before accepting Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s suggestion that the strategy of the Subaltern series “in claiming a positive subject-position for the subaltern might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times”’ (p. 105, citing SS IV p. 345). Gyanendra Pandey, a member, reads the 1988 close as Gramsci’s point: ‘“The subaltern cannot speak,” writes Gayatri Spivak, making, I suggest, much the same point’ (Ethnos, 1995; reprint p. 285, read). Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that the 1988 essay ‘brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies’ and ‘may have provided a major impetus’ for the gender and voice themes of Subaltern Studies IX (1996). Her own later account (‘The New Subaltern’, 2000, read): ‘Except in the work of Susie Tharu ... Subaltern Studies is not informed by feminist theory as such’ (p. 325), and of 1985, ‘Subaltern Studies had no need of such apologetics. But the theoretically inclined metropolitan identitarians did’ (p. 332). Later reading, labelled: Partha Chatterjee (2010; Morris volume, unpaginated) recalls first reading both essays in 1985 with ‘bewilderment’ and calls her intervention ‘the poststructuralist moment in Subaltern Studies’, adding that a changed political context also drove the shift. A critique from within, not a rejection: she joined the editorial collective in the 1990s. edge_389 (gender → subaltern) carries the same story under the gender entry; see the proposed relabel. Guha’s person edge (pe137_guha_rel_01, guha draft) cites the same 1985 essay as reception; this edge is hers.

proposed_edges.relationship: Foucault's account of power criticised as blind to imperialism and the international division of labour, and for an intellectual who lets the oppressed 'speak for themselves' while remaining transparent; his analyses of disciplinary institutions kept as useful (1988)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period text: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint, read in full). She takes as her object ‘Intellectuals and power: a conversation between Michel Foucault and Gilles Deleuze’ (p. 66), whose participants ‘systematically ignore the question of ideology and their own implication in intellectual and economic history’ (p. 66). In her summary of the conversation, ‘the oppressed can know and speak for themselves’ (p. 74); she adds ‘to Said’s analysis the notion of the surreptitious subject of power and desire marked by the transparency of the intellectual’ (p. 75). ‘Foucault is a brilliant thinker of power-in-spacing, but the awareness of the topographical reinscription of imperialism does not inform his presuppositions’ (p. 85); ‘The clinic, the asylum, the prison, the university - all seem to be screen-allegories that foreclose a reading of the broader narratives of imperialism’ (p. 86). She keeps part of his work: ‘what remains useful in Foucault is the mechanics of disciplinarization and institutionalization, the constitution, as it were, of the colonizer’ (p. 90), and calls his model of localized resistance ‘an admirable program’ that, universalized, ‘accommodates unacknowledged privileging of the subject’ (p. 85). Foucault’s position is given only as she presents it, from the translated conversation and Power/Knowledge; no reply was looked for (he died in 1984). Reception: Eagleton (1999, read) groups Derrida and Foucault as thinkers who ‘veer between a cult of theoretical “madness” ... and a more restrained, reformist sort of politics’, a criticism of her allies, not a defence of Foucault. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) carries her name with Stoler’s; see the optional relabel. Said’s separate critique of Foucault is pe137_said_rel_04 (said draft); she cites Said’s criticism and extends it (p. 75).
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The foucault person entry has no strands.

proposed_edges.relationship: Derrida's deconstruction, which she translated and introduced (1976), used and tested as a method for reading colonial texts and subaltern historiography, without being celebrated 'as feminism as such' (1976–88)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period texts. Translator’s preface to Of Grammatology (1976; read at p. lxxvii of the 1997 corrected edition): ‘To locate the promising marginal text, to disclose the undecidable moment, to pry it loose with the positive lever of the signifier; to reverse the resident hierarchy, only to displace it; to dismantle in order to reconstitute what is always already inscribed. Deconstruction in a nutshell. But take away the assurance of the text’s authority, the critic’s control, and the primacy of meaning, and the possession of this formula does not guarantee much.’ Subaltern Studies IV (1985): ‘This is the greatest gift of deconstruction: to question the authority of the investigating subject without paralysing him, persistently transforming conditions of impossibility into possibility’ (p. 336). ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (1985) sets ‘the lessons of deconstruction’ aside for the essay, choosing to ‘strategically take shelter in an essentialism’ (p. 244). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): ‘Derrida is hard to read; his real object of investigation is classical philosophy. Yet he is less dangerous when understood than the first-world intellectual masquerading as the absent nonrepresenter who lets the oppressed speak for themselves’ (p. 87); reading ‘Of grammatology as a positive science’, she reads him as placing the ethnocentric constitution of the Other as ‘Not a general problem, but a European problem’, and ‘As a postcolonial intellectual, I am not troubled that he does not lead me ... to the specific path that such a critique makes necessary’ (p. 89); ‘I have attempted to use and go beyond Derridean deconstruction, which I do not celebrate as feminism as such’ (p. 104); ‘In a certain way, then, the critique of imperialism is deconstruction as such’ (n. 47, p. 108). In-period reception: Eagleton (1999, read) calls Derrida ‘a consecrated figure for this book, about whom hardly a breath of criticism seems permissible’. Prakash (1992; reprint pp. 224–225, read) quotes her definition of deconstruction as an ‘impossible “no” to a structure, which one critiques, yet inhabits intimately’. Later reading, labelled: Chatterjee (2010) recalls that in 1982 the subalternists ‘did not imagine that Jacques Derrida ... could have anything remotely to do with Indian peasants’. Wikidata’s ‘influenced by’ (P737) lists Paul de Man, not Derrida; that is a Wikidata statement, not evidence here. Her translation’s publication dates (first American edition 1976, corrected 1997) are already checked on derrida_grammatology_corrected. edge_025 (derrida → post) tells her story under the group entry; see the proposed relabel.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Target is the new person entry, which has no strands.

proposed_edges.relationship: Chakrabarty uses 'Spivak's subaltern' as an analogy for the subject whom university history's transition narrative can only represent, the 'Indian' history that 'cannot speak itself as “theory”' (1992)
proposed_edges.map_label: ‘Spivak’s subaltern’ in the artifice of history, 1992
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chakrabarty’s in-period text. ‘Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History’, Representations 37 (1992), read (JSTOR copy; spacing restored): the antihistorical subject ‘cannot speak itself as “theory” within the knowledge procedures of the university even when these knowledge procedures acknowledge and “document” its existence. Much like Spivak’s “subaltern” (or the anthropologist’s peasant who can only have a quoted existence in a larger statement that belongs to the anthropologist alone), this subject can only be spoken for and spoken of by the transition narrative’ (p. 19, n. 52, citing ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ and her 1990 Socialist Review interview). He also borrows, ‘in Gayatri Spivak’s words’, ‘the feeling of community that belongs to national links and political organizations’ (p. 18, n. 48, citing the 1988 essay at p. 277; Williams and Chrisman reprint p. 72); she is among those thanked in the unnumbered first note (p. 23), and n. 43 (p. 25) credits her with an expression (‘personal communication’). Her side, in period: Subaltern Studies IV (1985) discusses his labour essays (pp. 331, 344) and sets them against the collective’s neglect of gender: ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357). The influence is bounded: Chakrabarty’s provincializing argument ‘follows directly’ from his work in Subaltern Studies (2000, p. 15; on edge_914), and the guha draft proposes Guha → Chakrabarty for the critique of the ‘pre-political’. This edge records one acknowledged borrowing in the 1992 programmatic essay, not a genealogy.

Her gender arguments in the texts read are addressed to Subaltern Studies (1985, pp. 356–363), to feminist literary criticism (‘Three Women’s Texts’, p. 243) and to ‘international feminism’ (1988, p. 84), not to gender history as a field; she has no gender roster row, and no in-period gender historian’s uptake was read. edge_389 (gender → subaltern) stays in place, with the relabel proposed below.

Not proposed. Her reading of The Eighteenth Brumaire (1988, pp. 70–74) uses Marx against Foucault and Deleuze (‘Marx is not working to create an undivided subject where desire and interest coincide’, p. 71); it is a use, not a critique, and she adds that Marx ‘himself rehearses an ancient subterfuge’ about the family (p. 74). A Marx edge would need a separate reading of A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, chapter 1.

proposed.relationship: Feminist critics press Subaltern Studies on women's place in its accounts of subaltern consciousness, labour and community, and gender becomes a theme of the series (1985–96)
proposed.evidence_note: Janaki Nair's 1990 review in International Labor and Working-Class History questions Chakrabarty's treatment of gender in Bengal labour (graph verification note; gender strand bengal_labor_gender; not re-read here). Spivak's 1985 and 1988 essays are her own edge (revision for postcolonial person entries). Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' 'brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies' and that Subaltern Studies IX (1996) made 'gender issues' a dominant theme, with Kamala Visweswaran's 'Small Speeches, Subaltern Gender' and Susie Tharu and Tejaswini Niranjana's 'Problems for a Contemporary Theory of Gender' (both unread). Spivak (2000, p. 325, read) names Tharu as the member whose work is informed by feminist theory. The arrow records criticism and its uptake within the series; it does not claim that the collective adopted a feminist programme.

proposed.relationship: Deconstruction taken into postcolonial historical criticism and disputed there by historians (1985–92)
proposed.evidence_note: Gyan Prakash, 'Can the “Subaltern” Ride?' (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint, pp. 224–227, read), defends deconstruction for historical writing under the heading 'Deconstructive Criticism and Historical Writing', reading Derrida's Of Grammatology and 'White Mythology' and answering O'Hanlon and Washbrook, who, as he quotes them, charge it with a 'residual positivism' and, in his paraphrase, with treating the historian's intervention in the past as illegitimate (p. 225, citing their p. 198). O'Hanlon and Washbrook's own text is known here only through its first page and notes (pe132_ohanlon_washbrook_1992) and through Prakash's quotations. Rosalind O'Hanlon (1988; reprint p. 80, read) reads the Subaltern series' recovery of the subject as a 'strategy' whose 'limitations have yet to receive any proper public discussion'. Spivak's own use is the separate derrida → Spivak edge.

edge_025.alternative: Leave edge_025 unchanged if reviewers prefer the group edge to keep naming Spivak as its example.

new_sources.title: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, “Three Women’s Texts and a Critique of Imperialism”, Critical Inquiry 12, no. 1 (Autumn 1985): 243–261.
new_sources.citation: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, “Three Women’s Texts and a Critique of Imperialism”, Critical Inquiry 12:1, “Race,” Writing, and Difference (1985): 243–261. doi:10.1086/448328.

verification.note: Read pp. 243–245 in a copy of the JSTOR PDF (cover sheet: Critical Inquiry 12:1, pp. 243–261, stable URL 1343469) hosted on a University of Warwick module page. Crossref gives the DOI, volume, issue and pages. Passages used: the opening sentence on imperialism as 'England’s social mission'; 'particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism' (p. 243); 'the lessons of deconstruction' and 'strategically take shelter in an essentialism' (p. 244). The readings of Jane Eyre, Wide Sargasso Sea and Frankenstein (pp. 246–261) were not read.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period (1985) essay: imperialism in nineteenth-century British literature and feminist criticism.

new_sources.title: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: Toward a History of the Vanishing Present (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1999), chapter 3, “History”.
new_sources.citation: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, A Critique of Postcolonial Reason (Harvard University Press, 1999), ch. 3, “History” (revised “Can the Subaltern Speak?”); reprinted in Rosalind C. Morris, ed., Can the Subaltern Speak? Reflections on the History of an Idea (Columbia University Press, 2010), part one.

verification.note: The revised essay was read in the Columbia University Press e-book of Morris (2010), part one, headed '“Can the Subaltern Speak?” revised edition, from the “History” chapter of Critique of Postcolonial Reason'; the e-book has no page numbers. Passages used: 'in the first version of this text, I wrote, in the accents of passionate lament: the subaltern cannot speak! It was an inadvisable remark'; Bhubaneswari Bhaduri 'was not a “true” subaltern'; the revised sati sentence ('imposed upon those women a greater ideological construction ... by an ignorant (but sanctioned) synecdoche'). spivak_speak.note: Re-read for the Spivak person entry: the reprint's pp. 66–104 in full and notes pp. 104–111. The copy is the reprint in Patrick Williams and Laura Chrisman, eds., Colonial Discourse and Post-Colonial Theory (1993), where it is chapter 4 at pp. 66–111 and its opening is abridged ('[ ... ]'); its first page cites the 1988 Nelson and Grossberg pagination, pp. 271–313. Two 1988 page anchors were found in other texts: the 'feeling of community' passage (reprint p. 72) is 1988 p. 277 (Chakrabarty, 'Artifice', 1992, n. 48), and the closing 'The subaltern cannot speak' (reprint p. 104) is 1988 p. 308 (Sunder Rajan, in Morris, ed., 2010). The reprint's last lines are OCR-damaged; their wording was checked against the unpaginated 1988 text reprinted in Morris (2010). Pages used: p. 66 (the subject of the West); p. 70 (the two senses of representation; intellectuals 'represent themselves as transparent'); p. 71 ('an essentialist, utopian politics'); pp. 76–78 (epistemic violence; the question); p. 79 (Guha's autonomy: 'I cannot entirely endorse'); pp. 82–84 (the female subaltern 'even more deeply in shadow'); pp. 85–86 and 90 (Foucault); pp. 87–89 and 104 (Derrida); p. 90 ('information retrieval'); pp. 92–97 and 102 (sati); p. 104 (close); n. 47 p. 108 ('the critique of imperialism is deconstruction as such'); n. 65 p. 109 (Lata Mani).

derrida_grammatology_corrected.note: Translator's preface re-read for the Spivak person entry (preface pp. ix–lxxxvii per the contents page; corrected-edition pagination). Quoted: 'To locate the promising marginal text, to disclose the undecidable moment, to pry it loose with the positive lever of the signifier; to reverse the resident hierarchy, only to displace it; to dismantle in order to reconstitute what is always already inscribed. Deconstruction in a nutshell' (p. lxxvii). Whether the 1976 first edition paginates the preface identically was not checked.

pe132_chakrabarty_artifice_1992.note: Re-read for the Spivak person entry. Quoted: 'in Gayatri Spivak’s words', 'the feeling of community that belongs to national links and political organizations' (p. 18; n. 48 cites 'Can the Subaltern Speak?', 1988, p. 277); the antihistorical subject 'cannot speak itself as “theory”' and, 'Much like Spivak’s “subaltern”', 'can only be spoken for and spoken of by the transition narrative' (p. 19; n. 52 cites the 1988 essay and her 1990 Socialist Review interview). Spivak is thanked in the unnumbered first note (p. 23) and credited in n. 43 (p. 25).

pe137_spivak_deconstructing_1985.note: Re-read in full for the Spivak person entry (same DLI scan; pages from its page-number file and running heads). Pages added to those in the guha draft: 'plotted as confrontations rather than transition' (p. 330); Chakrabarty's labour essays discussed (pp. 331, 344); 'This is why I hope to align them with deconstruction' and 'the greatest gift of deconstruction' (p. 336); the strategy 'might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times' (p. 345); 'No such luck for the “female”' (p. 357); 'Male subaltern and historian are here united' (p. 358); 'woman is the neglected syntagm' (p. 359); the 'red herring' sentence (p. 360); 'not a task that the group should fairly be asked to perform' (p. 361); 'Envoi' (p. 363).

pe137_ohanlon_recovering_1988.note: Re-read for the Spivak person entry (Verso reprint pagination). Quoted: 'This, then, I think, is what Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak means when she speaks of the contributors’ use of “a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest”' (p. 80; n. 14, p. 113, cites SS IV p. 342), and the strategy's 'larger significance and, more importantly, its limitations, have yet to receive any proper public discussion' (p. 80); 'we should certainly hesitate before accepting Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s suggestion that the strategy of the Subaltern series “in claiming a positive subject-position for the subaltern might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times”' (p. 105; n. 83, p. 115, cites SS IV p. 345).
